1                II.   PURPOSE AND SUMMARY OF TESTIMONY

2    Q.   What is the purpose of your rebuttal testimony in support of the Stipulation?

3    A.   My rebuttal testimony responds to Staff’s opposition to the Stipulation, including

4         Staff’s Statement in Opposition and Staff’s testimony in opposition to the

5         Stipulation. I continue to support the Stipulation and recommend that the

 6        Commission approve it without modification.

 7   Q.   What are the main points of your rebuttal testimony?

 8   A.   My rebuttal testimony addresses three main points:

 9               First, the Stipulation satisfies the Commission’s criteria for approving

10        stipulations and serves the public interest. The Stipulation resulted from serious

11        bargaining among capable, knowledgeable parties. It benefits customers and the

12        public interest. And it does not violate any important regulatory principle or

13        practice.

14               Second, Staff’s opposition fundamentally conflicts with New Mexico law

15        and longstanding Commission policy favoring settlements. Staff’s opposition treats

16        Staff’s direct testimony as the benchmark for whether the Stipulation is reasonable.

17        That approach is inconsistent with the give-and-take required to settle a contested

18        rate case. Although Staff acknowledges that settlements may differ from litigated

 2           Stipulation with Staff’s preferred jurisdictional-allocation, class revenue-

 3           allocation, banding, rate-design, accounting, and cost-recovery positions. If the

 4           Commission were to accept Staff’s approach and adopt certain provisions of the

 5           Stipulation and reject others, it would result in parties withdrawing from the

 6           Stipulation and litigating this rate case. 2 Thus, the Commission can approve or

 7           reject the Stipulation, but the parties cannot be forced to agree to an amended

 8           version of the Stipulation.

 9                    Third, Staff’s argument that the Commission should use historical

10           jurisdictional allocators to allocate Future Test Year (“FTY”) costs conflicts with

11           New Mexico law, the Commission’s FTY framework, and the matching principle

12           that underlies cost-of-service ratemaking. This is a New Mexico FTY rate case.

13           Texas law does not apply here. Staff’s proposal would mismatch FTY costs and

14           revenues with historical allocation data, treat forecasted New Mexico load growth

15           inconsistently, and import Texas historical-test-year limitations into a New Mexico

16           retail rate case.

 3   Q.      What criteria does the Commission apply when reviewing a contested

 4           stipulation?

 5   A.      The Commission considers whether (1) the stipulation resulted from serious

 6           bargaining among capable, knowledgeable parties; (2) the stipulation, as a whole,

 7           benefits customers and the public interest; (3) the stipulation, as a whole, violates

 8           any important regulatory principle or practice; 7 and (4)s the settlement is fair, just,

 9           and reasonable. 8

10   Q.      Does the Stipulation satisfy those criteria?

11   A.      Yes. The Stipulation satisfies each of those criteria. It resulted from serious

12           bargaining among capable, knowledgeable parties. The Stipulation, as a whole,

13           benefits customers and the public interest. And the Stipulation, as a whole, does not

14           violate any important regulatory principle or practice. For those reasons, the

15           Stipulation is fair, just, reasonable, and in the public interest.
